title: Terminates TPS for Nepal
description_short: DHS announced the termination of Temporary Protected Status for Nepal.
description_medium: On April 26, 2018, the Department of Homeland Security announced that Nepal’s Temporary Protected Status designation would end. TPS let eligible Nepali nationals already in the United States remain and work temporarily after the 2015 earthquake made safe return difficult. DHS set a transition period before the protection expired, so the announcement did not mean immediate deportation. It began the process of ending a humanitarian immigration status for people covered by the designation.
description_long: The Department of Homeland Security announced on April 26, 2018, that it would terminate Temporary Protected Status for Nepal. The designation had followed the 2015 earthquake, which left conditions that made safe return difficult for eligible Nepali nationals living in the United States. TPS allowed qualifying people to remain and work temporarily while the designation was active; it was not permanent residence or citizenship. DHS provided a transition period before the termination took effect. That gave people time to seek another lawful immigration status or prepare to leave, but it did not guarantee that either option would be available to every TPS holder. The announcement therefore changed the legal position of the covered group over time rather than ordering removals on the day it was issued. The decision was part of the administration’s review of country-specific TPS designations and drew attention to how humanitarian protections can be ended even when recipients have built lives in the United States. The policy affected Nepali nationals who qualified under the designation; it did not change the status of every person from Nepal.

description_long: On November 1, 2019, President Trump issued the determination setting the fiscal year 2020 refugee admissions ceiling at 18,000. The annual ceiling establishes the maximum number of refugees the United States may admit through its resettlement program during that fiscal year. It is not a guarantee that the full number will arrive: applicants still pass through eligibility screening, referrals, security checks, and travel arrangements. The 18,000 limit was described as a record low and marked a further contraction of the U.S. resettlement program. Refugees are people outside their country who cannot safely return because of persecution or other qualifying circumstances; resettlement offers a route to protection for a small share of those displaced worldwide. A lower ceiling narrows that route, even if the eventual admissions total falls below the cap for other reasons. The determination set the administration’s formal limit for FY2020 and left the agencies to conduct the individual selection and processing work within it. The figure describes authorized capacity, not the number ultimately admitted that year.

title: Signs Executive Orders Targeting TikTok and WeChat

description_medium: On August 6, 2020, Trump signed separate executive orders targeting transactions involving TikTok owner ByteDance and WeChat owner Tencent. description_long: On August 6, 2020, President Trump signed two executive orders aimed at TikTok, owned by ByteDance, and WeChat, owned by Tencent. Both orders invoked national security and sought to prohibit specified U.S. transactions with the companies. The measures did not instantly remove either app from users’ phones; their practical effect depended on the transactions covered, implementing steps, and court review. The threatened restrictions put the platforms’ U.S. operations in doubt and raised questions about the government’s power to regulate communications services through emergency authorities. They also brought competing concerns into view: the administration’s security claims, the companies’ commercial interests, and the effects a broad restriction could have on users and speech. The orders were challenged in court, which complicated their implementation and kept the dispute from ending with the signing. The episode became an early example of the administration seeking to reshape the U.S. technology market through executive action directed at Chinese-owned companies. It records the orders and their stated targets; the signing alone did not mean that the proposed restrictions all took effect.

title: Ends ACA Cost-Sharing Reduction Payments
description_short: The administration stopped federal CSR payments to insurers under the Affordable Care Act.
description_medium: The Trump administration ended federal cost-sharing reduction payments to insurers on October 12, 2017. Under the Affordable Care Act, those payments reimbursed insurers for lowering deductibles and other out-of-pocket costs for eligible low-income customers. The legal requirement to provide the reductions remained, shifting the cost onto insurers and prompting responses such as higher premiums. The decision created immediate uncertainty for insurers and state regulators.
description_long: On October 12, 2017, the Trump administration announced it would stop reimbursing health insurers for cost-sharing reductions under the Affordable Care Act. The payments supported lower deductibles, copayments, and other out-of-pocket charges for eligible low-income enrollees who bought certain marketplace plans. The ACA requirement that insurers provide those reductions remained in force, so ending the federal payments did not remove the benefit from eligible customers. Instead, insurers had to account for the lost reimbursement when setting premiums and deciding which plans to offer. Some states and insurers responded by adding the cost to premiums for marketplace plans, a practice known as silver loading; the exact effects varied by state and plan. The decision followed the administration’s broader effort to reduce federal support for ACA implementation. It shifted a financing obligation and forced state insurance regulators to address uncertainty ahead of future enrollment periods. The payment termination was an administrative policy change, not a repeal of the ACA or an immediate cancellation of cost-sharing assistance.

description_short: The House impeached Trump for incitement of insurrection following the Jan. 6 attack.
description_medium: The House of Representatives impeached Donald Trump on January 13, 2021, charging him with “incitement of insurrection” after the January 6 attack on the Capitol. description_long: On January 13, 2021, the House of Representatives approved one article of impeachment charging President Donald Trump with “incitement of insurrection” after a mob attacked the U.S. Capitol on January 6. The vote included support from members of both parties and made Trump the first U.S. president impeached twice. The House’s action formally accused him of misconduct; impeachment alone does not convict a president or remove him from office. The Senate is responsible for conducting the trial and deciding whether to convict. It later acquitted Trump, so the House vote did not result in a Senate conviction. The impeachment followed the disruption of Congress as lawmakers met to count electoral votes from the 2020 election. The charge centered on Trump’s conduct before and during the attack, while criminal cases against individual rioters proceeded separately through the courts. The House vote therefore added a constitutional accountability proceeding to the aftermath of January 6, with the Senate’s later decision completing the process.

The order initiated that administrative approach, but the effect on insurers, states, and people enrolled in coverage turned on the specific rules and actions that followed. description_long: On April 16, 2019, President Trump vetoed a bipartisan congressional resolution that would have directed the removal of U.S. forces from unauthorized hostilities in Yemen. The veto did not declare war or resolve every question about the limits of presidential authority in future operations. It instead kept this specific congressional measure from taking effect. The dispute reflected a broader tension over who controls U.S. military involvement abroad: the president directing foreign policy and Congress exercising its constitutional powers over war and funding. The veto preserved the administration’s position while leaving the underlying debate over Yemen and war powers unresolved.

title: Matt Gaetz Nominated as Attorney General
description_short: Matt Gaetz Nominated as Attorney General
description_medium: In November 2024, Trump nominated Matt Gaetz to serve as Attorney General, a shocking selection that sent shockwaves through Washington. The nomination was widely seen as Trump choosing a loyalist willing to weaponize the Justice Department against his political enemies.
description_long: President-elect Donald Trump announced on November 13, 2024, that he would nominate Representative Matt Gaetz to be attorney general. Gaetz had recently been investigated by the department over allegations involving sex trafficking of a minor; federal prosecutors did not bring charges, according to NPR. The allegations were not a conviction, and the decision not to prosecute did not amount to a finding about every claim made in the investigation. A nomination also does not install someone in office: the Senate must confirm the nominee. Gaetz withdrew from consideration before confirmation amid questions about whether he could secure enough support. The selection drew attention because the nominee had been under investigation by the same department he was chosen to lead. Trump’s decision set off a brief confirmation fight over the department’s leadership and the standards for its top law-enforcement post.

description_long: President Trump signed Executive Order 14173 on January 21, 2025. Agencies had to implement the order through guidance, contract terms, and compliance reviews, and the order’s scope remained subject to legal challenges. The Federal Register text set out the administration’s policy direction; it did not itself document the eventual effects on every contractor or recipient. The order marked a major shift in federal requirements for contractors and established a new framework for reviewing DEI practices tied to federal funding.

title: EPA FY2026 Budget Request Cuts Superfund by 47%, Zeroes Discretionary Remedial Funding
description_short: EPA FY2026 Budget Request Cuts Superfund by 47%, Zeroes Discretionary Remedial Funding
description_medium: The Trump administration’s May 2, 2025, FY2026 budget request proposed reducing the EPA’s Hazardous Substance Superfund account from $537.7 million to $282.749 million, a cut of about 47.4%. description_long: The Trump administration’s FY2026 budget request, released May 2, 2025, proposed reducing the EPA’s Hazardous Substance Superfund account from $537.7 million enacted for FY2025 to $282.749 million. The $254.951 million decrease equaled about 47.4%. State and Tribal Assistance Grants support environmental programs managed by state, local, and tribal governments. The numbers were part of the president’s proposed budget and still required congressional action; they were not final appropriations or proof that cleanup work had stopped. The request would have shifted a large share of EPA funding away from these programs if enacted. The budget documents do not support the separate claim that Superfund tax receipts were 26% below projections.

description_long: In January 2018, The Wall Street Journal reported that Michael Cohen, Trump’s personal lawyer, had arranged a $130,000 payment to Stormy Daniels shortly before the 2016 presidential election. The episode joined campaign-finance questions with a personal allegation that Trump denied.

title: Trump Signs First Muslim Travel Ban — Airport Chaos Nationwide
description_short: Trump Signs First Muslim Travel Ban — Airport Chaos Nationwide
description_medium: On January 27, 2017, Trump signed Executive Order 13769, suspending refugee admissions for 120 days and barring entry for 90 days by nationals of seven predominantly Muslim countries. The order also indefinitely paused Syrian refugee admissions. It took effect immediately, leading to detentions and confusion at U.S. airports while travelers were in transit. Federal judges issued emergency orders limiting enforcement, and the administration later replaced the order.
description_long: President Trump signed Executive Order 13769 on January 27, 2017. The order suspended the U.S. refugee program for 120 days, halted Syrian refugee admissions indefinitely, and restricted entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen. Because it took effect immediately, travelers were stopped or detained at airports, including some people who already had permission to live in the United States. Lawyers and volunteers gathered at airports as federal judges issued emergency orders limiting parts of the policy. The administration later replaced the order with revised versions after litigation. The first travel ban triggered disputes over presidential immigration authority, religious discrimination, and due process. Its initial terms did not remain in effect unchanged: later orders altered the restrictions, and courts reviewed those policies on their own records. The episode began with an abrupt nationwide directive that left travelers, airlines, and immigration officials uncertain about who could enter the country.

title: Trump Repeatedly Calls Climate Change a Chinese Hoax
description_short: Trump Repeatedly Calls Climate Change a Chinese Hoax
description_medium: Trump repeatedly called climate change a hoax and claimed China had invented the idea to weaken U.S. manufacturing. His statements contradicted the scientific consensus that human activity is warming the climate. A 2017 New York Times report examined whether he continued to hold that view as his administration considered withdrawing from the Paris climate agreement.
description_long: Trump repeatedly dismissed climate change as a “hoax” and claimed that China had created the concept to weaken U.S. manufacturing. He first made the China claim publicly in 2012 and continued to repeat it during his political career. The statement cast climate science as a foreign economic tactic rather than a field of research based on measurements of temperatures, greenhouse gases, and other evidence. Scientific agencies, including NOAA and NASA, have documented human-caused warming. In 2017, The New York Times examined whether Trump still held the view as his administration considered leaving the Paris climate agreement. His comments were consequential because they came from a candidate and then a president with influence over federal climate policy and public debate. The claim that China invented climate change is unsupported by scientific evidence; researchers across countries have documented the warming trend and its causes. Trump’s remarks framed climate action as a threat to U.S. industry and challenged the basis for international efforts to reduce emissions.

description_long: In August 2016, Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort shared internal polling data and battleground-state strategy with Konstantin Kilimnik, a political consultant whom the Senate Intelligence Committee assessed had ties to Russian intelligence. description_short: Trump Bans AP from Press Pool Over 'Gulf of America' Refusal
description_medium: Beginning February 11, 2025, the White House excluded Associated Press journalists from the presidential press pool after the AP kept using “Gulf of Mexico” rather than Trump’s preferred “Gulf of America.” The restrictions blocked AP access to events and travel with the president. description_long: The White House began excluding Associated Press journalists from the presidential press pool on February 11, 2025, after the AP declined to change its style guide to call the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” The restrictions limited the news organization’s access to Oval Office events, Mar-a-Lago, and travel aboard Air Force One. The AP sued three administration officials, arguing that the government could not deny access because of the newsroom’s editorial choice. A federal judge ruled in the AP’s favor, but the White House responded with a revised press-pool policy that continued to limit the outlet’s access. The dispute raised a First Amendment question about viewpoint discrimination in a limited-access press pool. The litigation showed that a court ruling did not immediately restore the AP’s former access. title: New York AG Files $40M Fraud Lawsuit Against Trump University
description_short: New York AG Files $40M Fraud Lawsuit Against Trump University
description_medium: New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman filed a $40 million civil fraud lawsuit against Donald Trump and Trump University in August 2013. The complaint alleged that the program operated as an unlicensed school and misled thousands of students about its instructors and real-estate training. Trump denied wrongdoing and attacked Schneiderman publicly. The case settled in 2016 for $25 million, with Trump not admitting liability.
description_long: New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman sued Donald Trump and Trump University in August 2013, seeking $40 million in civil penalties and relief. The complaint alleged that the real-estate seminar business operated as an unlicensed educational institution and misled more than 5,000 students about the training they would receive. It challenged promotional claims that Trump personally selected instructors and that participants would learn his real-estate methods. Trump disputed the allegations and attacked Schneiderman publicly. The case settled in November 2016 for $25 million, shortly after Trump won the presidential election. Trump paid as part of the settlement without admitting liability. The agreement resolved the state’s claims but was not a trial finding that he committed fraud. It also covered students who had sued separately, bringing multiple disputes over the seminars into one settlement. The case became a prominent example of the legal scrutiny surrounding Trump’s pre-presidential business practices.

title: Arpaio Pardon for Contempt of Court
description_short: Arpaio Pardon for Contempt of Court
description_medium: Trump pardoned former Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio on August 25, 2017, after Arpaio was convicted of criminal contempt for violating a federal court order in a racial-profiling case. The order had barred Arpaio’s office from detaining people solely on suspicion of undocumented immigration status. Trump called him a patriot. The pardon ended the contempt case before sentencing and drew criticism over respect for court orders and equal protection.
description_long: On August 25, 2017, President Trump pardoned Joe Arpaio, the former sheriff of Maricopa County, Arizona. Arpaio had been convicted of criminal contempt after disobeying a federal judge’s order that his office stop detaining people based solely on suspicion that they were undocumented immigrants. The underlying case concerned racial profiling by the sheriff’s department. Trump praised Arpaio as a “patriot,” and the pardon came before sentencing. A presidential pardon forgave the federal contempt offense, but it did not erase the court’s findings about the sheriff’s conduct in the civil case. The Justice Department’s customary review process was bypassed, drawing criticism that the president was rewarding a political ally for defying a court order. Arpaio’s case became an early test of Trump’s use of clemency and raised questions about respect for judicial authority and equal protection. The pardon ended the federal contempt prosecution without a sentence being imposed.

title: Trump Threatens to Revoke NBC Broadcast License
description_short: Trump Threatens to Revoke NBC Broadcast License
description_medium: On October 11, 2017, Trump threatened on Twitter to revoke NBC’s broadcast licenses after criticizing its reporting. He asked why the FCC was not reviewing the network and called the coverage “fake news.” The president does not personally issue or revoke broadcast licenses; the FCC regulates individual stations under federal law. Press-freedom advocates warned that using licensing threats in response to unfavorable reporting could chill journalism, even though legal experts said the threat had no clear path to implementation.
description_long: On October 11, 2017, President Trump tweeted that NBC’s broadcast licenses should be challenged after criticizing reporting he disliked, including stories about North Korea and the U.S. nuclear arsenal. He asked why the Federal Communications Commission was not investigating the network and called its coverage “fake news.” Broadcast licenses are held by individual stations and administered by the FCC; the president cannot revoke them by personal order. The Associated Press reported that experts saw no practical basis for the threat to result in license loss. Even without direct authority, a president’s use of licensing threats against a news organization can put pressure on journalism and raise concerns about retaliation for editorial choices. The remarks prompted renewed debate over the independence of the media regulator and the limits of government influence over broadcasters. NBC did not lose a license as a result of the tweet, and the FCC did not open a proceeding based on Trump’s statement.

title: Camp East Montana: Beatings, Extrajudicial Killing, Enforced Disappearances at Fort Bliss
description_short: Camp East Montana: Beatings, Extrajudicial Killing, Enforced Disappearances at Fort Bliss
description_medium: A July 2026 Human Rights Watch and ACLU report described abuse at Camp East Montana, an immigration detention facility opened at Fort Bliss in 2025. description_long: A July 2026 report by Human Rights Watch and the ACLU documented abuse allegations at Camp East Montana, an immigration detention facility opened at Fort Bliss in El Paso in August 2025. The groups interviewed 71 detainees; 64 said they had experienced or witnessed beatings by masked guards without name tags. The report also described the January 3, 2026, death of Geraldo Lunas Campos, a 55-year-old Cuban detainee. He was restrained in solitary confinement after asking for medication and died by asphyxiation. A local medical examiner ruled the death a homicide. A Government Accountability Office review later found that required reports had not been provided and evidence connected to the incident was missing or destroyed. These findings describe interviews, a death investigation, and recordkeeping failures at the facility. They raised questions about use of force and oversight in immigration detention, while individual criminal responsibility remained for investigators and courts to determine.

description_long: On December 7, 2015, then-candidate Donald Trump issued a campaign statement calling for a “total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States” until officials could determine how to address security concerns. The Court’s ruling concerned a revised government policy and its record, not the exact language of the 2015 campaign statement. The proposal became an early and defining immigration pledge in Trump’s presidential campaign and set the stage for later disputes over the travel restrictions.
